questions.q: Why is "momentum works" not a usable hypothesis for testing?
options: Because momentum has been proven false
Because it is too vague to be falsifiable — almost any result could be interpreted as confirming it
Because momentum signals can't be coded in Python
Because it only applies to currencies
questions.explain: A usable hypothesis must be specific enough that a particular result would prove it wrong. "Momentum works" has no such specificity, so it can't really be tested, only confirmed after the fact.

questions.q: What is a "kill criterion" in the context of hypothesis-driven strategy research?
options: A rule that stops the backtesting software if it runs too long
A specific, pre-decided result that would make you discard the idea rather than keep tuning it
The maximum drawdown a live account can sustain
A legal requirement for publishing research
questions.explain: A kill criterion is decided before looking at results — it's the outcome that would make you walk away from an idea instead of continuing to adjust it until it looks better.

questions.q: Why should the signal definition, success metric, and kill criteria be written down before running any backtest?
options: It's a regulatory filing requirement
It guards against hindsight bias — the tendency to rationalize, after seeing a result, that a chosen parameter "obviously" made sense all along
It makes the code run faster
It is only useful for team communication, not for the individual researcher
questions.explain: The lesson explains that writing a hypothesis down beforehand is a defense against your own brain's tendency to retroactively justify choices that were actually made because they produced a better-looking result.

questions.q: What is a "holdout period" and why does it matter?
options: A period where no trading is allowed by regulation
Historical data deliberately set aside and not examined until final testing, so later results aren't contaminated by having been seen during development
The time it takes to fit a model
The minimum holding period for a position
questions.explain: A holdout period is data reserved and genuinely untouched during strategy development, so that testing on it later provides a cleaner, less biased check of whether the strategy generalizes.

questions.q: Skipping the hypothesis-writing discipline and instead repeatedly tweaking a signal until a backtest looks good is an early form of which problem, covered in depth later in this course?
options: Transaction cost modeling
Overfitting / data snooping
Execution algorithm design
Risk budgeting
questions.explain: Iteratively adjusting a rule until it matches the one history you've already seen is exactly the overfitting / data snooping problem, which Chapter 4 (Realism in Backtests) covers in full.
